recurrent_mechanisms.mechanism: Repeated RAG retrieval exposure does not by itself become semantic adoption, temporal permission or common-pool-like authority.
All four trajectories stop before a material version-review/repair chain forms and leave application state unchanged.

divergence_patterns: G2 is the clearest retrieval-control case: the same task-level RAG hit bundle is exposed repeatedly across 52 cycles, yet no adoption/action chain develops.
G3–G5 reach comparable nondevelopment horizons without supported C/P/R.
boundary_interpretation: Retrieval visibility is not equivalent to system semantic authority. A retrieved item must be read/adopted/transformed into downstream decision state before it can participate in C or R.
This cohort is therefore directly relevant to the distinction between external retrieval memory and a shared common pool that agents treat as operational state.
cross_group_semantic_synthesis.cohort_conclusion: RAG X5-T1 provides a strong negative control for the memory-layer hypothesis: repeated retrieval availability alone does not produce Dynamic C or R. Across four frozen trajectories, retrieved historical/version context never becomes an operational semantic lineage or downstream permission effect. This supports treating RAG as an external evidence carrier rather than assuming it functions as a system common pool merely because information is repeatedly available.

constraints: Cell-level Layer-C verdicts are sealed and are not modified by cohort synthesis.
Boundary-excluded natural cells remain excluded rather than imputed.
Dimension recurrence is descriptive across frozen stochastic realizations; it is not a rerun-based reproducibility claim.
